title: Sodium Supplementation and Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia during Prolonged Exercise
population: Starters and finishers of the 161-km Western States Endurance Run (body weight, questionnaire, post-race serum sodium)
findings: Questionnaire completed by 74.5% of 376 starters; blood sample from 61.1% of 296 finishers; 53.0% of finishers did both.
Hyponatremia incidence among finishers 6.6%; 93.9% used sodium supplements.
Post-race serum sodium directly related to sodium supplement intake rate (r = 0.24, P = 0.0027) and inversely related to body weight change (r = -0.19, P = 0.010).

No difference in sodium supplement intake rate between hyponatremic and normonatremic finishers; none of the hyponatremic finishers lost > 4.3% body weight; hyponatremic finishers were not distinguished by other runner characteristics, drinking strategies, or nausea/vomiting.

Conclusion: low sodium intake from supplements has minimal responsibility for hyponatremia during continuous exercise up to 30 h; overhydration is the primary characteristic; avoiding overhydration is the most important prevention.
limitations: Observational, self-reported intake, weak correlations, near-universal supplement use (restricted contrast), single event; the positive sodium-intake correlation means sodium may modestly help, which authors interpret as small.
implications: Treat sodium as secondary: no rule that sodium supplements prevent EAH; advise not to overdrink.
If sodium targets are shown, use Tiller's range (> 575 mg/L of fluid) labelled as taste/cramp/comfort support.
Add alert for 20-30 h races with heavy fluid intake: EAH risk is not fixed by any sodium rule.

verification.notes: Crossref match; numbers confirmed in the Europe PMC abstract. Sample size 376 is starters; 296 finishers.
